entries.title: White Sox GM Chris Getz succeeds, survives at 'grueling' trade deadline
entries.summary: <p>BOSTON — Chris Getz had been through two trade deadlines as the White Sox’ general manager, but neither compared to the one he just went through with a first-place team.</p><p>“It is very grueling,” he said Wednesday from a makeshift workout area in the Fenway Park concourse. “I wake up in the middle of the night, I wake up early in the morning, and your mind is going.</p><p>“It’s definitely a stimulating time, but because probably of the lack of sleep and the actual work that it entails, it takes its toll. But you’ve got enough adrenaline to work your way through it. And then, when it’s over, you feel like you’ve been hit by a Mack truck.”</p><p>Getz stood as he spoke in the cramped space with weights and machines protected by black curtains, so he seemed to have recovered enough to keep his balance. And as tired as he was, he felt good about what he and his staff accomplished before the deadline at 5 p.m. Monday.</p><p>The Sox acquired a three-time All-Star starting pitcher in Luis Castillo, a two-time Gold Glove center fielder in Brenton Doyle, a reliable reliever in Huascar Brazoban and a veteran catcher in Joey Bart. They had to part with some quality prospects, but none of their coveted ones.</p><p>“We accomplished our goal,” Getz said. “We got better in the areas that we needed to get better in. We built some depth. We got controllable players. We maintained the top-end talent in our organization. It has been a long road to get where we’re at. We feel very good about the process that we’ve been able to carry out.”</p><p>Some of those good feelings come from feedback from other organizations. Getz said clubs were supportive of the players he acquired and understood what his plan was. It reinforced the relationship-building aspect of trading that Getz said is imperative.</p><p>“So much of this is building a rapport with whomever you’re dealing with,” he said. “It may not be a GM or an assistant GM or a president. Oftentimes, organizations are dividing and conquering because you’re talking about so many different players. You might have someone broker a deal, and you come in late to get something to the finish line.</p><p>“The more that I’m doing this, the more value I put in that. In a world that has become highly objective, highly analytical, there’s a difference between valuing the players and actually getting to the finish line in a negotiation. And it takes a combination of all of those things.”</p><p>Getz said trade talks with other teams begin weeks before the deadline, with clubs explaining what they’re trying to accomplish. He said this deadline was unique in that, with a glut of teams in playoff contention, many still were deciding whether they were buying or selling.</p><p>“So not only are we waiting for that clarity, they’re looking for clarity themselves,” Getz said. “It’s a waiting game: Which direction are you going to go? But most of those teams are planning for different scenarios, in that you earmark certain players that you would have interest in.”</p><p>Even when there is clarity, a deal could be made at the oddest of hours, as was the case with the Mets and Brazoban, the late-looming 36-year-old who’s under club control through 2029, when he’ll be 39.</p><p>That trade went down after midnight Monday morning. Getz said he still was looking for another starting pitcher at the time — he had acquired Castillo from the Mariners on Saturday night — but he wasn’t comfortable giving up what it would’ve cost.</p><p>“So therefore, OK, let’s take a step back, let’s assess other pitching talent that’s out there; in this case Brazo,” he said. “He has control, it’s an upgrade for our bullpen, what we felt like was a fair price for someone of his level. And that’s why we chose to go that path. The timing of it just so happened to be fairly late.”</p><p>Getz said he was open to acquiring rental players, but “it became very clear that our systems just didn’t match up for some of those guys.” And as important as it was to Getz that he not disrupt the chemistry in the clubhouse, it was equally as important that he not trade away the Sox’ top prospects.</p><p>“We wanted to maintain the integrity of that, continue to fuel this organization,” Getz said. “We feel like we’ve done that.</p><p>“So I can sleep well now, not purely because I’m exhausted.”</p><div class="PageListL" entries.title: Portillo’s laying off staff at Oak Brook headquarters
entries.summary: <p>Hot dog chain Portillo’s cut 18% of its corporate staff as it continues a strategic reset amid lower sales across restaurants, the company announced on Wednesday.</p><p>The chain known for Chicago-style hot dogs and Italian beef sandwiches has roughly 140 employees at its Oak Brook headquarters at 2001 Spring Road.</p><p>Portillo’s also cut some field management roles. But its layoffs didn’t affect restaurant workers at its 109 fast casual locations nationwide.</p><p>Portillo’s had about 7,800 workers across the U.S. as of December, according to its 2025 annual report.</p><p>"While never an easy decision, it is imperative that we examine areas of the business where we can operate more efficiently and ensure our resources and future investments are directed at the right priorities. These actions, along with other efficiencies, will support our long-term growth strategy,” CEO Brett Patterson said in a news release.</p><p>Portillo’s made the cuts on July 31, according to a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. There was no announcement yet under the Illinois Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification Act, but there is often lag time before layoffs appear on the state’s WARN website. Employers must report layoffs of 25 or more full-time employees, under WARN.</p><p>The job cuts will cost Portillo’s about approximately $1.1 million in restructuring charges, according to an SEC filing.</p><p>“There were no restaurant-level team members impacted, and you can expect that Portillo’s will continue to produce the high-quality service and craveable food that our loyal fans and guests have appreciated for the past 63 years,” Portillo’s said in an emailed statement.</p><p>In April, the company raised some menu prices by 2% to cope with inflation. Portillo’s noted higher commodity prices for beef and produce in its second quarter earnings call on Wednesday.</p><p>Portillo’s announced net income fell $2.9 million to $7.2 million in the second quarter. Same-restaurant sales — sales at restaurants open for at least 24 months<b> </b>— decreased 1.2%, or $2.2 million, in the quarter.</p><p>On Tuesday, the company named Kevin Kalicak its chief financial officer, effective Sept. 7. He was most recently Olive Garden’s senior vice president of finance.</p><p>It’s the latest management change at Portillo’s as part of a “strategic reset” announced last fall. Patterson was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/restaurants/2026/02/12/portillos-brett-patterson-ceo" >named CEO</a> in February, after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/work/2025/09/23/portillos-ceo-michael-osanloo-resigns-immediately" >Michael Osanloo</a> resigned from the role in September.</p><p>Portillo’s, launched as a hot dog trailer in 1963, has <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/money/2026/02/24/portillos-slowing-national-expansion-weaker-sales" >scaled back</a> an ambitious national expansion amid flagging sales.</p><p>In 2026, the company opened eight new locations, all in Texas. It plans to open a Downtown restaurant at <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/06/08/portillos-open-michigan-avenue-restaurant" >304 N. Michigan Ave.</a> in the fourth quarter. Portillo’s also expects to open a location in Wrigleyville at 3519 N. entries.title: Man charged in 2021 River North homicide
entries.summary: <p>A man has been charged in the 2021 fatal shooting of a man in River North, according to Chicago police.</p><p>Rashawn Ward, 31, faces a charge of first-degree murder and one count of unlawful use of a weapon by a felon for allegedly possessing a firearm as a convicted felon, police said. He was arrested Tuesday.</p><p>The 33-year-old was standing next to his vehicle about 3:50 a.m. in the 800 block of North Orleans Street Sept. 18, 2021 when Ward, inside a blue SUV, is alleged to have opened fire, police said. The man, shot once in the chest, was taken to Northwestern Memorial Hospital, where he died. He was later identified as Royal Shorts of Hammond, Ind.</p><p>Ward is due back in court for a detention hearing Thursday, police said.</p>

entries.title: Nothing goes right for White Sox in shutout loss to Red Sox
entries.summary: <p>BOSTON — Nothing is going right for the White Sox against the Red Sox, on the mound, in the field and at the plate.</p><p>Sean Burke struggled in the ballpark of his youth, Sam Antonacci made two costly mistakes and the White Sox couldn’t dent Sonny Gray in a 4-0 loss to the Red Sox on Wednesday. The White Sox have lost all five games against the Red Sox this season by a combined score of 33-4. </p><p>Burke left after 4 ⅓ innings, allowing two runs, five hits and two walks. The Sutton, Massachusetts, native grew up going to Fenway Park and had supporters in attendance.</p><p>“That adds to the frustration,” Burke said. “It’s one of the few times a bunch of my friends and family, people I grew up with, can come watch me. Not to have my best stuff tonight sucks.</p><p>’’From the get-go, the breaking balls weren’t really there. I was really just pitching off my four-seam, two-seam and cutter today, which makes it hard against a lineup like that.’’</p><p>Antonacci made it hard for himself. In the third, he tried to score from second on a grounder to third baseman Caleb Durbin, whose throw pulled Willson Contreras off first base. But Contreras had plenty of time to nab Antonacci at home. </p><p>’’Looking back at it, the whole play was right in front of Contreras,’’ Antonacci said. ’’The amount of years he’s been in the league, that’s an easy play for him. It’s a ball you got to stay put at third on, let Colson [Montgomery] hit us in.’’</p><p>In the seventh, Antonacci misread a fly ball in medium left field and wasn’t in position to make a good throw to get Andruw Monasterio tagging from third.</p><p>’’Tough read on my end,’’ Antonacci said. ’’Had to jump at the very end and wasn’t able to get behind it. I think if I get behind that ball a little bit better, just the way it was hit off the bat, right away I thought it was a broken bat and he kind of flared it into left field. I was coming in right away and just came in a little too hard.’’</p><p>Of course, none of it mattered much because the White Sox couldn't score. Gray allowed three hits and two walks in six innings while striking out eight, getting plenty of swing-and-miss on his sweeper.</p><p>‘‘Sonny Gray had really good stuff tonight, especially to lefties,’’ said White Sox manager Will Venable, who stacked the lineup with five lefties and two switch hitters. ‘‘You saw a lot of spin early [in counts] in the zone that we didn’t fire on. And then later in counts, [we chased] the spin below. He had a lot of different ways he was attacking us, and we just didn’t have any solutions.‘‘</p><p>The White Sox maintained a three-game lead over the Guardians and a four-game lead over the Twins, both of whom lost. At 59-54, the White Sox are the only team in the American League Central above .500.</p><p><b>NOTE:</b> The White Sox designated outfielder <b>Austin Hays</b> for assignment. Hays, who signed a one-year, $6 million deal, had been on a rehab assignment at Triple-A Charlotte for a strained left calf and was hitting well, but White Sox manager <b>Will Venable</b> said he fell entries.title: Sky's DiJonai Carrington finding her form faster than expected in return from injury
entries.summary: <p><b>DiJonai Carrington</b> didn't want to put too much pressure on herself to instantly return to her old form — after all, it had been nearly a year since she'd played in a game.</p><p>Maybe that's partly why her comeback has gone so smoothly.</p><p>In her first three games back, she's averaging 11.7 points off the bench while bringing her usual defensive intensity.</p><p>She’s been pleasantly surprised.</p><p>"I feel like each game I've felt myself getting a little more comfortable trying something new or just being able to take bumps and contact and stay on balance a little bit more," Carrington told the Sun-Times at shootaround Wednesday.</p><p>Carrington waded in with her 3-point shot and pull-up in the first two games, then burst into the paint in her third. She shot a game-high 12 free throws against the Mercury, though she wasn't pleased about missing five of them.</p><p>"Getting to the line don't matter if you don't make them," she said. "So focusing on that as well."</p><p>Carrington wants to be an efficient scorer and keep adding to her game the rest of the season. But overall, she defined success as being able to play without thinking about her injured foot. She said she's been able to do that "in waves," though occasionally she'll catch herself thinking about it on a closeout.</p><p>That particular challenge hasn't slowed her drive to lead, however. She already feels responsible for the team's defensive coverages down the stretch, an area she noted has hurt the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> in clutch games. She thinks being more attentive to body language can help.</p><p>"When [other teams] do go on the runs, I think we show it," Carrington said. "I'm not saying that we don't keep fighting on the court. I think just how we come to the bench, we might overreact, as opposed to just — basketball is a game of runs. They're gonna go on runs. We're gonna go on runs. We have to stay even."</p><p>Overall, returning to the fold has validated for Carrington what her teammates and coaches have been saying all season: This team has fight.</p><p>"We never feel like we're out of the game," she said.</p><p><b>Dual minds</b></p><p>With the Sky and Sparks both entering Wednesday's game holding only an outside shot at the playoffs, each team is approaching the rest of the season with a mix of pragmatism and presence.</p><p>The Sky sat down together after the All-Star break to map out what making the playoffs would require — likely winning 12 or 13 of their final 17 games. But they also want to take it a day at a time, trying to view every matchup as a "one-game season."</p><p>Sparks coach <b>Lynne Roberts</b> is threading the same needle. She said she hasn't done the math on how many games the Sparks need to win — but her players are "not dumb" and know the kind of run they'd need to go on to make up ground.</p><p><b>Stevens returns</b></p><p>Forward <b>Azura Stevens</b> is back with the team after missing four games for personal reasons. Coach <b>Tyler Marsh</b> said she'll be ramping up in the coming days. She did not play against the Sparks.</p>

entries.title: Teen killed in North Center e-scooter crash remembered as a 'goofy' boy who was 'always there for everybody'
entries.summary: <p>Alex Blacio was everyone's "rock."</p><p>He was a steady presence in his family, according to his relatives. The teen played volleyball through middle and high school — becoming the captain of the varsity volleyball team at Lake View High School last year, where he was happy to play wherever he was needed — and would often meet up with his middle school friends to play at open gyms.</p><p>Monday, the 16-year-old was riding an e-scooter northbound in the 4100 block of North Western Avenue around 3:35 p.m. when he lost control and was hit by a tractor-trailer, Chicago police said in a statement. He was taken to Illinois Masonic Hospital, where he was pronounced dead, police said.</p><p>It was his third day at his first job, and though he hadn't been scheduled for work, he was eager to pick up another shift to help out his family, according to his older sister, Andrea Blacio.</p><p>"He showed so much love, he was always there for everybody," she said. entries.title: Injured White Sox catcher Kyle Teel saves Davis Martin from tipping pitches
entries.summary: <p>BOSTON — White Sox catcher Kyle Teel has a skill that came in handy Tuesday night when starting pitcher Davis Martin wasn’t fooling the Red Sox in the first inning.</p><p>“I would say I’m good at picking up patterns, good at pattern recognition,” Teel, who’s on the injured list with a sprained left ankle, told the Sun-Times. “Kind of a big role that I feel like I’ve had on the IL has just been helping our defense, helping our pitchers, trying to protect them as much as possible.”</p><p>While the Red Sox were pounding Martin for six runs and six hits — including back-to-back homers, the first being a grand slam — Teel was watching closely from the dugout, trying to detect whether Martin was tipping pitches.</p><p>“It’s a lot easier from the dugout,” Teel said. “When you’re behind the plate, you’re really focused on catching the ball, trying to frame pitches, throwing guys out, blocking balls. It’s hard to really key in on certain things. But it’s one of those things like, once you see it, you see it.”</p><p>And once Teel saw it, he went to work confirming it.</p><p>“Once I think there’s something, I log it in a notebook and see how many are accurate to what I was putting down,” he said. “If I have a page full of checkmarks, I give it to the coaching staff. They do a really good job, as well, finding tips on guys. It’s a good thing to have as a catcher. It’s something I brought from college, just learning how to do that.”</p><p>It made a difference. After the first, Davis retired 12 of the next 14 batters he faced, inducing mostly soft contact outside of a solo homer in the fifth. But he only lasted two batters into the sixth, departing with 91 pitches, because of that long first inning due to the tipping.</p><p>“Generally, there’s [tipping from] the glove,” Sox pitching coach Zach Bove said, “but guys do different mannerisms, stuff like that, that you would think would never be a thing. For whatever reason, guys create these patterns, and other teams are trying to look at the patterns.”</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" entries.title: Man loses job after falling ill from cyclosporiasis
entries.summary: <p>It had been years since Edgar Mercado had eaten at a Taco Bell restaurant.</p><p>But early last month, his 14-year-old son wanted some, so he took him to the one near Belmont and Milwaukee avenues.</p><p>“We ate there. A couple of days later, I got sick. My stomach was in pain, like somebody hit me with a hockey stick. I threw up a few times and then the diarrhea. I was dizzy and I couldn’t get out of bed,” said 50-year-old Mercado, who lives in the Jefferson Park neighborhood.</p><p>Once he was able to get to a doctor, Mercado said it was confirmed he had cyclosporiasis, caused by the microscopic parasite cyclospora.</p><p>“I couldn't go to work. I sent them a copy of my situation, and they just let me go,” said Mercado, who had been working for more than a month at a Jewel distribution facility in Melrose Park.</p><p>Mercado plans to sue Taco Bell and Taylor Farms for his illness and loss of wages.</p><p>“We want to make sure that each of our clients are fully and fairly compensated for the losses they've suffered. The second thing we're looking for is to figure out exactly how this happened. How the feces got in the lettuce,” said Ron Simon, Mercado’s attorney, who has not yet filed a lawsuit.</p><p>Simon said his firm represents 300 Illinois residents who claim to have gotten sick from cyclospora.</p><p>“We want to make sure we force Taylor Farms and Taco Bell to take steps to make sure that no one else gets hurt in the future,” Simon said.</p><p>Neither Taco Bell nor Taylor Farms could be reached for comment.</p><p>According to University of Chicago Medicine, cyclospora is a parasite that's very hard to eradicate. Those infected can experience loss of appetite, abdominal cramping and bloating, fatigue, low-grade fever and increased flatulence. Symptoms start two to 14 days after consumption and can last for several weeks.</p><p>“Cyclospora outbreaks are not new. We do see cyclospora outbreaks occur from time to time related to contaminated soil and produce,” Dr. Aniruddha Hazra, associate professor of medicine and director of the infectious disease fellowship program at University of Chicago Medicine, said.</p><p>“I think the concern that many of us have in infectious disease and public health is that the extent at which this outbreak has been allowed to expand is certainly unusual,” Hazra said.</p><p>Hazra said the parasite is very hard to kill. The only way to be safe in eating spinach, for example, is to cook it.</p><p>According to the Illinois Department of Public Health, there have been 995 confirmed or probable cases of cyclospora, with 58 hospitalizations but no deaths, as of Tuesday. In Cook County alone, there have been 112 probable and confirmed cyclosporiasis cases</p><p>Simon, Mercado's attorney, said the federal government could do more.</p><p>“This administration made the decision to cut back on jobs and workers at the [Centers for Disease Control and Prevention] before the outbreak. As a result, there's not enough people at the CDC to track and keep up with these cases,” Simon said. “They’re working overtime as it is. We just don’t have enough people out there trying to solve the outbreak, and that’s why it’s taking so long.”</p><p>A month after heading to Taco Bell for lunch with his son, Mercado said he’s feeling better. Mercado added he did not take any medication to get well, other than drinking Pedialyte.</p><p>“It’s been about four days now that I’ve been back to normal. It feels good to be back to normal,” Mercado said. “I was praying to God every day to take this away from me.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="mailto:mpuente@wbez.org" target="_blank" ><u></u></a><br></p>

entries.title: Former Sky guard Ariel Atkins settles in as everything changes around her
entries.summary: <p>Nothing about Ariel Atkins’ fresh start with the Sparks has gone as planned.</p><p>Not one thing.</p><p>Kelsey Plum, the superstar guard she was supposed to pair with in the backcourt? Traded to the Mercury at the deadline.</p><p>Raegan Pebley, the general manager who took the big bet on Atkins? Fired weeks earlier.</p><p>And the team that talked about championship aspirations during training camp? Dropped to 10th place after losing to the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> on Wednesday night.</p><p>Ownership now says they're open to taking a step backward to move forward.</p><p>Atkins understands that uncertainty is part of the business. She also believes everything happens for a reason.</p><p>“It is what it is,” Atkins told the Sun-Times at shootaround Wednesday. “People move. I could not be here next year. I could have been a part of the [Plum] trade. You just never know with sports.</p><p>“Happy to still be here, just where my feet are and locking into who I want to be, not only as a basketball player but as a person. Just staying focused on that. Staying prayed up. Not being upset or angry.”</p><p>Atkins’ transition to the Sparks hasn’t been easy. Her scoring is down, and she is shooting a career-low 30.1% from three.</p><p>But everyone around the Sparks describes Atkins the same way her coaches and teammates did in Chicago: steady, coachable and too valuable defensively to take off the floor, even as she struggled to find her offense.</p><p>That offense began to come when she faced the Sky in late June, finishing with 17 points and six assists. Over the next seven games, Atkins averaged 11.7 points and four assists while shooting 35.1% from three on 5.3 attempts per game — numbers much closer to what she has produced throughout her career.</p><p>“I finally calmed down and started finding my way,” Atkins said.</p><p>Sparks coach Lynne Roberts can see the difference in the way Atkins moves.</p><p>“It’s been fun to see her figure it out,” Roberts said. “You can physically see the burden off her shoulders in terms of trying so hard. Now she’s relaxing and playing in a much more efficient way.”</p><p>Atkins said at the start of the season that she considered re-signing with the Sky. But after a short stint in Chicago that also did not go as planned, she decided she needed a fresh start.</p><p>The Sparks believed her experience and defense could help push them toward contention. Now, nearly every Sparks player has to be wondering: Will this be a long-term home?</p><p>Atkins is the Sparks’ second-highest-paid player, with a $3.41 million deal that runs through 2028. But the person who signed her is gone.</p><p>Farhan Zaidi, special adviser to Sparks owner Mark Walter, recently told the Los Angeles Times that the organization has “to be open for anything” and that “everything has to be on the table.”</p><p>“We pushed in a lot of chips this year, and we had good reason to do that, but the reality is it hasn’t gone as we’d hoped or expected,” Zaidi said.</p><p>While the front office plots its next moves, Atkins is staying in the present. She is learning more about her new teammates — apparently they are Marvel crazy, so they went to see the new Spider-Man together. The day before facing the Sky, the team toured the Obama Presidential Center.</p><p>None of them doubted Atkins would find her footing.</p><p>“It just takes a little time to get your feet wet, chemistry with the girls and everything,” Sparks guard Rae Burrell told the Sun-Times. “We’ve been patient with her and believed in her from the jump.”</p>
